title: The Stopgap: Governing by Deadline
hook: Legislatures are supposed to pass budgets. When they cannot agree, many just extend last year's spending a few months at a time — and the deadline becomes the real negotiation.
key_points: Most governments cannot spend money without a legislative appropriation, so if the spending law lapses, funded operations stop.
A stopgap — in the U.S. Congress, a continuing resolution — keeps agencies funded at roughly existing levels for a set period instead of settling the full budget.
It converts a substantive fight over what to fund into a scheduling fight over when the next cliff falls.
In September 2026, per NPR, the House approved legislation extending federal funding through mid-December, pushing the next deadline past the midterm elections.
Timing is itself a political choice: whoever sets the expiry date decides who holds leverage, and under what political conditions, at the next vote.
The cost of governing this way is planning — agencies and contractors budget in short, uncertain increments.
content_html: A legislature's core power is the purse: money can only be spent if the legislature has authorized it. That makes the funding bill the one thing that absolutely has to pass — and when agreement on the full budget is out of reach, the common workaround is to extend the old one for a few more months.
extra_html: That short extension is called a continuing resolution in the U.S. Congress, and the pattern is familiar in other systems too: rather than resolve what to fund and at what level, the legislature keeps spending roughly where it is and sets a new deadline. NPR's Sam Gringlas reports that in early September 2026 the House approved legislation extending federal funding through mid-December, with NPR's Eric McDaniel noting beforehand that the bill was top of the agenda as the House returned from recess. Notice what the choice of date does: it moves the next funding cliff past the midterm elections, which changes who will be negotiating and under what pressure. That is the recurring lesson — a stopgap does not settle a disagreement, it reschedules it, and the scheduling is part of the bargain. The price is paid in planning: agencies, grantees and contractors have to operate in short, uncertain increments rather than against a settled annual budget. (This card describes the U.S. federal budget process specifically; other systems have their own provisional-spending rules.)

related.hook: A government's budget is its values written in numbers — and taxation is how it raises the money to act at all. Follow the money to understand the priorities.

flashcards.prompt: What does a stopgap funding bill (a continuing resolution) actually do?
flashcards.back_html: It extends existing spending levels for a fixed period instead of enacting a full budget — keeping agencies open while postponing the substantive fight over what to fund.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the expiry date on a stopgap bill politically important?

choices.text: It decides when the next shutdown fight happens, and therefore who has leverage then
It sets the tax rate for the following year
It determines which agencies are permanently abolished

flashcards.explanation_html: A stopgap does not resolve the disagreement, it reschedules it — so choosing the date is choosing the political conditions of the rematch.

flashcards.prompt: Why does funding lapse shut down government operations at all?

choices.text: Agencies generally cannot spend money without a legislative appropriation
Employees legally resign when a budget expires
Courts automatically order agencies to close

flashcards.explanation_html: The power of the purse is the mechanism: no appropriation, no legal authority to spend, so funded activity has to stop.
